title: FrameRouter: Frame Budget Routing for Long-Video Understanding on Video-MME-v2 and Beyond
claim: Uniform budgets waste or starve evidence across questions of differing difficulty; routing adaptive budgets keeps the same average cost.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, uniform vs adaptive with router and shared downstream model
description: The figure has two rounded panels. The left panel, titled 'Uniform Budget' in blue, shows three video-strip inputs: an easy local cue, a default question and a hard temporal reasoning question. Each has an arrow to the same-size row of colored squares. The labels under them read 'Wasted' for the easy question, 'OK' for the default and 'Insufficient' for the hard one, with a red warning icon. The right panel, titled 'FrameRouter' in orange, feeds the same three inputs into a central 'Evidence-Demand Router' box with a tree icon. Three colored arrows lead out: teal for fewer frames, blue for default and orange for more frames. They merge into a 'Frozen VLM' box. A balance-scale icon with 'Same Average Budget' sits at the bottom. Color coding is teal, blue and orange, and the eye goes first to the two panel titles.
caption: Overview of fixed-mean frame-budget routing. Uniform inference gives every question the same visual budget despite heterogeneous evidence demands. FrameRouter routes each question to an appropriate frozen budget policy using question-only signals, while preserving the same dataset-level average budget.
abstract: Long-video question answering benchmarks like Video-MME-v2 typically evaluate systems under a uniform frame budget for every question, despite stark variation in the evidence each query actually demands. We analyze this mismatch on Video-MME-v2 and find that different question subsets prefer different frozen frame-budget policies, while uniformly increasing the frame count does not reliably improve all metrics. These findings motivate fixed-mean frame-budget routing, a controlled inference setting in which each question may receive a different frame budget while the average budget matches a uniform reference. We introduce FrameRouter, a training-free test-time framework that combines an evidence-demand router, a budget-constrained allocation rule, and a frozen bank of frame-sampling policies. By controlling how much visual evidence each question receives while leaving the underlying samplers unchanged, FrameRouter is orthogonal to query-aware frame selection. Across Video-MME-v2 and several long-video understanding benchmarks, FrameRouter improves long-video question answering by using the same average visual budget more selectively across questions. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/FrameRouter.
